text_blocks.snippet: Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome (KTS) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by a combination of three main features: port-wine stain birthmarks, abnormal blood vessels (including varicose veins), and overgrowth of soft tissue and bones, often affecting one limb. The severity and combination of these features can vary significantly from person to person.
snippet_highlighted_words: port-wine stain birthmarks, abnormal blood vessels (including varicose veins), and overgrowth of soft tissue and bones, often affecting one limb

list.title: Port-wine stain birthmarks:
list.snippet: These are reddish-purple birthmarks that are often the first noticeable sign of KTS, appearing on the skin due to malformed capillaries.
Varicose veins: Enlarged, twisted veins that can be visible under the skin.
Venous malformations: Abnormalities in the deeper veins, potentially causing pain, swelling, or skin breakdown.
Capillary malformations: Abnormalities in the tiny blood vessels (capillaries).

list.title: Limb hypertrophy:
list.snippet: Overgrowth of bones and soft tissues, most commonly affecting one leg, which can lead to a difference in size and length between limbs.

list.title: Lymphatic system abnormalities:
list.snippet: Malformations in the lymphatic system can lead to swelling (lymphedema) and fluid buildup in the affected limb.
Pain: Can be caused by varicose veins, swelling, or bone overgrowth.
Skin infections (cellulitis): Due to compromised skin and lymphatic system.
Blood clots: Increased risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and other clotting issues.
Bleeding: From abnormal capillaries near the skin surface.
Hip dislocation: Can occur in some cases.
Eye problems: Such as glaucoma or cataracts, have been reported in some individuals.
Fusion of fingers or toes: Sometimes occurs in conjunction with limb overgrowth.
KTS can affect individuals differently, with some experiencing only a few mild symptoms while others have more pronounced and extensive issues, according to Stanford Health Care.
The severity of symptoms can also change over time, with some features becoming more apparent during childhood or adolescence.
There is no cure for KTS, but treatments are available to manage symptoms and prevent complications.
